task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: team defensive trait stability and reliability
counter strategy: best and avoid defensive approaches
methodological_questions: Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across seasons (test-retest reliability)?
How reliable are half-to-half change scores at team-season sample sizes, given that a difference score carries noise from both halves?
Does regression to the mean or selection on extreme H2-H1 values threaten inference about a persistent defensive trait?
Is the 120-team-season sample large enough to detect a reliable team-level trait, and at what effect size?
Are defensive measures confounded by opponent quality, pace, lineup, or scheme labels?

historical_evidence.finding: Connector teammate-path quality Q_p split-half reliability (n=102 connectors). Pearson r=+0.215 (p=0.0297), Spearman rho=+0.242, Spearman-Brown about 0.355, ICC(player-season)=0.216 with 78.4% of variance within player. Recorded as too low to treat Q_p as a stable scoutable trait; failure mechanism A_unanswerable, limited by low measurement reliability. Not a defensive or H2-H1 study; relevant only as an analogous reliability warning for a split-half trait at similar sample size.

Defensive scheme change within and across games using inferred labels (523 cells, 440 pairs, 52 series). Within-game change 61.0%, cross-game change 67.7%; 99.0% of units show a change; transition matrices near-uniform. Documentation caveat: the inferred label cannot separate real defensive adjustment from the offense executing differently. Limited by label error.

Agent Test B: LLM counter selection versus the deterministic BEST tier on 3 suppression triggers. Agreed with BEST 1/3; picked AVOID 2/3; disagreements were right 2/2 by H2 PPP (BEST 1.650, agent 1.154, AVOID 0.642). Record notes 230+ disagreements would be needed. [prior work]'s observed_verdict is 'inconclusive'; failure type A_unanswerable, limited by small sample.

Adaptation versus generic counter (W4), n=1,539 triggers. BEST counter equalled the generic best available in 78.3%; suppression-specific in 21.7%. When the defense suppressed the generic best (4.7%, 73 cases), the specific counter was chosen 39.7% of the time. Positive result; limited by sample size in [prior work]. Concerns counter choice, not the H2-H1 trait of a defense.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Split-half reliability of a derived per-player differential as a stable trait
failed_approaches.why: Split-half r=0.215 (Spearman-Brown about 0.355) and ICC 0.216 with most variance within-player. [prior work] concludes the measure is too unreliable to act on as a stable trait at n=102. Analogous risk for a defense-level H2-H1 measure.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferred defensive scheme-change labels as a measure of defensive adjustment
failed_approaches.why: Near-uniform transition matrices and near-universal change flags are consistent with label noise. The inferred label cannot separate defensive adjustment from offensive execution differences. Recorded as LABEL_ERROR and untestable.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Agent-based counter selection validated on very few triggers
failed_approaches.why: Only 3 triggers; [prior work] states that 230+ disagreements would be needed. Verdict recorded as inconclusive, failure type A_unanswerable, limited by small sample.

evidence_establishes: No retrieved record tests whether a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait. No retrieved record reports a team-level defensive H2-H1 result.

A split-half reliability study of a derived play-based differential at n=102 ([prior work][prior work]) found reliability too low to treat as a stable trait, with most variance within-unit. This is a direct caution for any split-half or half-to-half design on this data.
Inferred defensive labels in this project have shown label-error signatures ([prior work][prior work]), so any defensive measure built on inferred labels needs validation before use.
Counter-selection work ([prior work][prior work]) shows that BEST-tier counters usually coincide with the generic best available, which matters for any 'best' or 'avoid' framing of the question.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is stable across seasons, since no retrieved record measures season-to-season reliability of this quantity.
The reliability of H2-H1 change scores for team defenses at 120 team-seasons, since no retrieved record analyses this sample.
Whether the retrieved records' sample sizes (102, 3, 1,539 triggers) are comparable to a 120 team-season design. They are not the same units or measures.
Whether any defensive effect survives opponent-quality, pace, or lineup adjustment.
The validity of the 'best' and 'avoid' counter classification as a measure of defensive quality.
own_inferences: H2-H1 change is a difference of two noisy half-level estimates, so its reliability is lower than that of either half alone. With about 120 team-seasons, a team-level trait would need a large effect to show reliability above the noise floor.

Four regular seasons of 30 teams gives about 120 team-seasons. Playoff samples are much smaller, and the 2025-26 regular season is only complete from 2026-04-13, so the data version must be frozen before analysis.
A plausible reliability ceiling is about the level recorded in SF-[prior work] (about 0.2 to 0.35), which would make a 'reliable trait' claim hard to support without a multi-season design.

A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is probably confounded by opponent strength, schedule, injuries and in-game lineup or score effects (for example garbage time or fatigue), none of which the retrieved records address.
uncertainties: The data catalog and the exact definition of a team's defensive effect on H2-H1 were not retrieved. No follow-up read_family call was made, so the full text of the retrieved records is unverified beyond the summaries shown.
Whether defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions support a stable per-team defensive measure is unknown.
The status of [prior work][prior work] is recorded as 'untestable'; its observed_verdict is 'inconclusive', which is reported in the finding text rather than as the status.
Whether the 'reliable team trait' claim should be read as test-retest reliability, cross-season persistence, or predictive validity is not specified in the question.
No historical record addresses playoff versus regular-season differences or the 2025-26 partial data.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records did not test the question. They did, however, supply a directly relevant warning: a split-half reliability analysis of a derived differential at n=102 ([prior work][prior work]) came out too low to treat as a stable trait, and inferred defensive labels show label-error signatures ([prior work][prior work]). Together with the reliability arithmetic in the own inferences, these records changed the decision from a plain test of the trait to a reliability-first design, and to a recommendation not to proceed as posed.

blocking_constraints.text: Half-to-half and difference-score reliability is likely low at team-season level. SF-[prior work] found reliability of about 0.2 to 0.35 for an analogous split-half measure.
120 team-seasons is unlikely to give adequate power to show a reliable team-level trait in H2-H1 change, especially with playoff subsamples much smaller.
Selecting defenses by extreme H2-H1 values would inflate apparent persistence through regression to the mean.
Opponent quality, pace, lineup and score-state effects can move H2-H1 change independently of the defense.
Any defensive scheme or play-type label built from inferred events may be noisy, as SF-[prior work] indicates.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record answers whether a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait. SF-[prior work] is a related split-half reliability study of a different player-level measure, with untestable status and low reliability. SF-[prior work] is an untestable defensive-label study with label-error caveats. SF-[prior work] is an underpowered counter-selection test recorded as untestable, with verdict inconclusive. SF-[prior work] is a supported counter-choice result that does not address the H2-H1 trait.

risks.text: H2-H1 change is a difference of two noisy half-level estimates. Reliability is expected to be low, and SF-[prior work] found a comparable analogue too unreliable to use.
About 120 team-seasons across four regular seasons, with smaller playoff subsamples, is probably insufficient to detect a modest reliable team-level effect.
Ranking or selecting teams on H2-H1 change in one period and reusing that selection in another will inflate persistence estimates through regression to the mean.
Opponent strength, schedule, pace, lineup, injuries and score-state (garbage time, fatigue) can drive H2-H1 change without any defensive trait.
Defensive and play-type labels derived from inferred events may not separate defensive action from offensive execution, as SF-[prior work] notes.
Rule changes, roster turnover, and the partial 2025-26 season may make defensive effects non-stationary across the four seasons being pooled.
Several defensive metrics, half definitions, and subgroup cuts (regular season vs playoffs) could be tried; without correction, one may appear reliable by chance.
If most team-level differences in H2-H1 change are noise, a 'reliable trait' claim would have a low prior and a high false-positive rate under loose criteria.
Half definitions (clock, period, overtime, and possession counting) and the join between play-by-play and derived possession records could introduce errors.

design.estimand: Not proceeding as posed. The minimum viable test first estimates the reliability of a team's defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 change: the between-team variance component over within-team noise, across seasons, with a stated reliability threshold.
design.unit: Team-season (defense) for the reliability estimate; opponent possession or game for the underlying H2-H1 outcome.
design.sample: Regular seasons 2022-23 to 2024-25 (complete) and 2025-26 only after its completion on 2026-04-13, giving about 120 team-seasons. Playoffs are reported separately because their samples are much smaller. Freeze the data version before analysis.
design.power: Not yet computed. Before any test, run a simulation of the split-half and cross-season reliability at 120 team-seasons, and report the minimum detectable reliability. Proceed only if the design can distinguish reliability of at least a pre-stated threshold (for example ICC of 0.5) from zero with adequate power.
design.controls: Adjust for opponent offensive and defensive strength, pace, possession count, lineup and rotation, injuries, and score state or garbage time. Use a mixed model with team and opponent random effects. Use pre-specified half definitions and validate the derived possession joins.
design.falsification: The trait claim is falsified if the cross-season reliability (ICC or test-retest) falls below the pre-stated threshold, or if the effect disappears after opponent and lineup adjustment. A placebo run using shuffled half labels or shuffled opponents should give null reliability.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register a single primary reliability metric and one primary threshold. Treat regular season and playoffs as separate pre-specified analyses, and correct any secondary metrics for multiple testing.
design.decision_rule: Proceed to a trait claim only if the pre-registered reliability threshold is met with a confidence interval excluding the null, after adjustment, and the placebo and falsification checks pass. Otherwise report the question as untestable or not supported at this sample size.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API files for 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular seasons and playoffs; 2025-26 regular season only after 2026-04-13 completion; 2025-26 playoffs only after 2026-06-21 completion. Freeze the version and record the derived possession graph build used.
